title: Treasury auction cycle and the month-end bond trade
hypothesis: Treasury ETFs cheapen before auctions and recover after (H5), and long duration earns a premium over month-end (H6).
question: Treasury notes and bonds have been found to cheapen in the days before a scheduled auction and recover afterwards. Separately, Treasury trading surges on the last day of each month. Does either show up strongly enough in the ETFs we already trade (IEF, TLT, hedged with SHY) to pay for itself, with orders at the next open?
prior: The auction result comes from 1980–2008 data, so nearly all of our 2007–2026 window is out of sample. Calendar effects are easy to keep free of look-ahead, but also among the most mined rules in finance, so the bar was set high: mean gross return of at least 28 bp per round trip to go on, and a deflated Sharpe counted against 9,500 calendar rules.
citations: Lou, D., Yan, H. & Zhang, J. (2013). Anticipated and Repeated Shocks in Liquid Markets. Review of Financial Studies 26(8), 1891–1912.
Sullivan, R., Timmermann, A. & White, H. (2001). Dangers of data mining: the case of calendar effects in stock returns. Journal of Econometrics 105(1), 249–286.
Federal Reserve Bank of New York, Liberty Street Economics (2024). End-of-Month Liquidity in the Treasury Market.
method: Auction dates from Treasury's Fiscal Data auction records (2,793 note and bond auctions), checked against Treasury's published cadence by tenor and year, with reopenings separated from new issues. 10-year auctions trade IEF; 20- and 30-year auctions trade TLT.

H5: a duration-neutral pair (short the target ETF, long its trailing 252-day beta in SHY) from five days before the auction to the auction day, then reversed for six days. A pre-auction window never starts before the auction was announced. 2009 on.
H6: long TLT from the open two trading days before month-end to the open of the next month's first trading day. 2007 on.

Three variants written down in advance (H5 on every auction, H5 on new issues only, H6). Kill test first: mean gross return per round trip below 14 bp stops a variant; 28 bp is needed to go on to the full gate. Costs 7 bps per unit traded.
verdict_reason: All three variants stopped at the kill test, so the full gate never ran. H5 on every auction averaged −3.7 bp gross per round trip (998 trips, t −0.8); on new issues only, +8.5 bp (t +1.1). Splitting the trade shows why: the cheapening into auctions is there (+14 bp on every auction, +24 bp on new issues), but the recovery afterwards loses money (−22 bp and −7 bp), and the hedge costs far more than either phase earns. H6, month-end TLT, was the strongest: +24.7 bp gross (t +3.1, +10.7 bp net), growing from +13.7 bp in 2007–2014 to +29.8 bp since 2021, but under the 28 bp bar set in advance for a heavily mined calendar rule, so it did not go on.
lessons: Half of a published effect can survive while the other half fails: the cheapening before auctions showed up, the recovery after did not.

A duration-neutral pair built from ETFs is costly to trade. TLT moves about six and a half times as much as SHY, so hedging it means trading about fifteen units per round trip, about 107 bp in costs against 14–24 bp gross.
A calendar rule that is positive, significant and growing (month-end) can still be too small to matter after it is counted against everything that has been mined.

rows: (c) H6, long TLT over month-end, 2007 on
